notes.claim: In an IT system the supply is isolated from earth, and the first earth fault should not cause any disconnection.
Marine insulated systems exist to prevent the immediate loss of an essential service from an earth fault.
In the earthing letters, T stands for earth (from the French Terre), N for neutral and I for isolated.
In an IT system the source transformer is isolated from earth while the installation's exposed conductive parts are connected to earth electrodes.
In a TN system the first earth fault is interrupted by the circuit's overcurrent protection, a breaker or fuse.
In an IT system the first earth fault should not cause any disconnection, and the earth-fault current is measured in milliamps.
Two-wire unearthed distribution was introduced to prevent the immediate loss of an essential service resulting from an earth fault.
An IT supply's star point may instead be connected to earth through a high impedance, commonly 1500 ohms or more, which still counts as IT.
On an IT system with a first earth fault, the healthy phases rise to root three times the normal phase voltage.
In an IT system the first earth fault passes only milliamps and causes no disconnection.
Equipment on an insulated system is rated at 173% of the phase voltage, the line voltage, so its insulation can hold a first earth fault.
A system called ungrounded is in reality coupled to ground through the distributed capacitance of its phase windings and conductors.
With no direct path back to the source's neutral, Eaton's 480 V example returns the first-fault current through the distributed capacitance of the two unfaulted phases, and only 1.04 A flows.
Eaton gives about 1 A of continuous charging current for roughly 10 microfarads on a 277 V system.
In an IT system the larger the system, the smaller the impedance between the active conductors and earth.
A second earth fault on a different live conductor is a short circuit between active conductors through earth and the protective bonding conductors.
The Electrical Installation Guide says it is conventional to double the loop impedance of a circuit when working out a second fault.
The IEC 60364-4-41 text recommends that a first fault be eliminated with the shortest practicable delay.
BS 7671 sets requirements for a second fault on an IT system, similar to TN systems, in Regulation 411.6.4.

An insulation monitor injects a very low frequency a.c. or a d.c. current, applying a voltage between the supply transformer's neutral point and earth to read the installation's insulation resistance to earth.
Bender says classification societies require an insulation monitoring device on each isolated system, to monitor continuously and alarm at abnormally low levels.
Guidance disagrees on the alarm level: Bender's booklet sets about 100 ohms per volt, its white paper calls 500 ohms per volt typical, and Schneider suggests 500 to 1,000 ohms.
notes.contested: Bender's booklet says set the alarm at about 100 ohms per volt, a Bender white paper calls 500 ohms per volt a typical critical value, and Schneider's Cahier 178 suggests an absolute 500 to 1,000 ohms.

notes.claim: The IEC 60364-4-41 text recommends that a first fault be eliminated with the shortest practicable delay.
Germanischer Lloyd rules: an insulation monitor on ships mains alarms below 50 ohms per volt of the operating voltage.
Bender: passive methods such as the three-lightbulb method cannot detect symmetrical failures.
An insulation monitor reads the total resistance, adding the resistive leakage of all outgoing lines in parallel to earth.
Earth lamps: three lamps between the phases and earth form a balanced load on a sound network, all lit with the same brilliance.
At an insulation fault, one of the three earth lamps is short-circuited by the fault impedance.
Insulation monitoring devices are not to be connected in parallel: one per connected system.
The larger the system in terms of leakage capacitance, the longer an insulation monitor takes to measure.
Humidity can lower the general level of insulation resistance without a single fault.
Some national standards recommend a first alarm setting 20% below the insulation level of the new installation.
Earth lamps are switched in only to test: setting the earth-lamp switch to TEST earths the star point of the lamp circuit.
On an insulated DC bus with healthy insulation, the two pole-to-earth voltage readings are each half the bus voltage.
On an ungrounded DC system the bus with the lower ground resistance has the lower voltage to ground.
Once one DC pole is connected to ground, a short follows if the other pole is also shorted to ground.
On an insulated DC bus, two earth lamps, one from each pole, each glow at half voltage; with the negative shorted to earth, the lamp on the positive glows at full brightness.
A ground detector can be a voltmeter switched between each pole and earth; a difference between the two readings shows an imbalance.
An electronic ground detector is a balanced bridge of equal resistors, and it alarms once the bridge becomes imbalanced.
To give an indication, a ground detector adds a connection to earth: it adds the fault it is trying to detect.
Full bus voltage on one pole-to-earth reading and zero on the other means a direct short to earth on the pole that reads zero.
A slight difference between the two pole-to-earth readings means a partial short to earth.
When several pieces of equipment with their own ground detectors are connected to one DC system, their detector circuits add in parallel.
Worked case: on a 100 V bus with 500 kOhm on the other pole, a pole whose insulation falls to 51 kOhm reads 9.26 V to earth (100/(500+51)x51).
DC power systems are normally ungrounded: both the positive and negative buses are insulated from earth.
Symmetrical insulation faults, about equal on both poles, are common in DC systems and control circuits.
In theory a single earth fault on an ungrounded DC system passes no leakage current, but stray and filter capacitors give leakage paths until they charge.
People who assume a floating DC bus is not connected to earth can be electrocuted working on it.
Bender gives touch voltages below 50 V AC or 120 V DC as safe for persons.
Ship automation and most other systems on board run on a 24 V DC control voltage.
Those capacitive leakage paths close once the capacitors' charge reaches steady state.
A live-tracking method clamps a probe on each feeder to measure its earth leakage current without interrupting distribution.
An insulation fault locator sends a test current pulse through the live conductors, the fault and the earth wire, and clamps on each circuit detect it.
To find a fault, engineers isolate circuits one at a time, with essential services covered, until the reading recovers.
Insulation measurement is the test of insulation resistance in the switched-off, de-energised system.

A clamp on each feeder at supply frequency is not reliable on a network with many feeders, some highly capacitive, because a short faulty feeder's earth current is hard to tell from a long capacitive feeder's.
Fault tracking uses a low-frequency signal so the network's leakage capacitance does not disturb it, though not below 2.5 Hz, where a magnetic sensor struggles to detect it.
Shutting down distributions one by one is hard at sea: not every system can be switched off, and the fault can disappear because the faulty load has already switched off.
An insulation monitor cannot measure insulation faults in loads that are switched off.
The locator's test current is seen by every measuring current transformer on the faulty circuit's path.
The locator limits its test current to a maximum value.
A portable locating set injects a locating current of 1 to 25 mA and reads it with clamps.
Each fault-location sensor is a toroidal current transformer around all the conductors of its circuit.
Insulation measurement (a dead test) and insulation monitoring (live) are easily mixed up.
Equipment likely to influence an insulation resistance test, or be damaged by it, is disconnected before the test.
An insulation monitor's maker says to disconnect the monitor before checking insulation.
Ship rules measure a switchboard's insulation resistance at a DC voltage of at least 500 V.
Common causes of earth faults on ships are water in junction boxes and deck lights, damaged cables, and insulation breaking down in motors and heaters.
Eaton reports that measured line-to-ground voltages of 1200 V or higher in its cases of intermittent ground faults on ungrounded systems are not uncommon.
notes.contested: Eaton says arcing ground faults on ungrounded low-voltage systems give measured line-to-ground voltages of 1200 V or more, while the IMarEST paper says such overvoltages are not a problem on marine systems because of heavy damping.

notes.claim: Industry has many documented cases of multiple equipment failures, such as motors, across an entire 480 V ungrounded system while a ground fault was being found.
The IMarEST paper says such overvoltages are not a problem on marine systems because of their higher losses and heavy damping.
A drive's internal EMC filter capacitors connect the supply network to ground potential.
An IT system with a latent first fault behaves exactly like a grounded system.
When an arcing earth fault's current reaches zero, the arc goes out, and because the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees, the phase-to-earth capacitance is at its peak voltage at that moment.
Once the arc is out, nothing charges or discharges the capacitance, so the phase-to-earth voltage stays where it was when the arc went out.
Half a cycle after the arc goes out, the phase's voltage to earth reaches twice its first value.
In Eaton's chain of restrikes the star point moves to three times the first phase-to-earth voltage, and the phase reaches four times it.

The restriking carries on until some device fails, typically one with a lower impulse level such as a control transformer, starter coil, motor winding or dry-type transformer, which then shorts the phase to earth for good.

The IMarEST paper says marine dielectric losses are much higher at the kilohertz frequencies involved, and cable losses alone sometimes damp the system past critical, so oscillatory overvoltages cannot occur.
ABB's instructions say to check a drive's compatibility with an IT supply and disconnect its EMC filter and ground-to-phase varistor.
With its EMC filter disconnected for an IT supply, a drive does not meet the EMC requirements of IEC 61800-3.
On an IT supply feeding drives, use a permanent insulation monitoring device compatible with non-linear loads.
On an AC system with galvanically connected DC parts, such as drives, those DC currents distort an insulation monitor's measurement.
High capacitive leakage disturbs insulation monitors that inject AC, and the tracking of a first fault.
Wherever possible, all work on electrical systems should be done with the system dead.
Once one rail is referenced to the chassis, by a fault or a slip, the chassis becomes a return path.
High-voltage ship systems are usually earthed through a resistor, which limits fault current to a few amps and avoids the overvoltages that can build up in a fully insulated HV system.
A touch voltage below 50 V AC or 120 V DC keeps persons safe.
Equipment on an insulated system is rated for 173% of its phase voltage, the line voltage, so it holds a solid first fault.

A surge limiter between an IT supply's neutral and earth, close to the MV/LV transformer, earths the LV network at once if the transformer's windings break down, so the LV side cannot rise to MV potential.
Once a large overvoltage has shorted the surge limiter, the insulation monitor reports it just as an insulation fault, and the cartridge is replaced.
